01 — Sightseeing

Monuments & Museums

London's national museums and galleries are free, every day — you only pay for special exhibitions. The paid landmarks below are the ones genuinely worth the money, with the cheapest way to see each one. Ratings are average visitor scores (Google/Tripadvisor, 2026). The £ marks show what you'd actually pay.

Ratings: ★ average visitor score out of 5 Price: £ = under £10 · ££ = £10–25 · £££ = £25+ Free tip: every paid landmark below has a free way in — read the card.

🏛️
★★★★★ 4.7
Great Russell St, Bloomsbury WC1B 3DG · Free

Good to know: the free national museums are the British Museum, National Gallery, National Portrait Gallery, Tate Modern, Tate Britain, Natural History Museum, Science Museum and the V&A — free every day, with only temporary exhibitions ticketed. The Science Museum is the one that asks you to book a free ticket; the British Museum and Natural History Museum recommend it at busy times. Free viewing platforms: Sky Garden, Horizon 22 and the Garden at 120 (120 Fenchurch St, no booking at all — just turn up). And new for 2026: the London Museum opens in the restored Smithfield General Market on 28 November 2026 — free entry.

Tax tip: UK prices already include 20% VAT — the ticket price is the price, and there's no tipping at the counter. Unlike many European cities, Britain currently has no tourist VAT-refund scheme at the airport (it was dropped in 2021; a return is a political proposal, not law), so don't budget for a refund. You can still claim VAT relief if a shop ships your purchase directly to your home country as an export. Also: the UK is now the only major shopping destination in Europe without visitor tax-free shopping, so leave room in the suitcase rather than the budget.
Best days & hours: most West End stores run Mon–Sat 10:00–21:00 and Sun 12:00–18:00 (Oxford Street Sundays are the quietest time all week — genuinely). Weekday mornings beat weekends everywhere. Market stalls are largely cash-free now, but small vintage traders still prefer it.

Market hack: the perfect London weekend is Saturday — Borough Market at 08:00 before the crowds, Broadway Market or Maltby Street for lunch, then Portobello Road in the afternoon. On Sunday, do Columbia Road flowers (before 11:00), walk to Brick Lane and Petticoat Lane (both open from 09:00–10:00), then finish at Spitalfields. Monday is the dead day: Borough is shut and the weekend street markets are gone — that's the day to book the paid landmarks instead. Hours shift with the seasons and holidays, so check the market's own page the day before.

Getting there without a car: everything here is rail-or-Tube reachable, which is the big London difference from a US city — ICON at The O2 and London Designer Outlet are straight Jubilee-line rides (tap contactless, no booking); Bicester Village is a direct Chiltern Railways train from Marylebone; Ashford is 38 minutes on the high-speed line from St Pancras. Book advance train tickets and an off-peak day return costs a fraction of the walk-up fare. Timing: outlets are busiest Saturday 11:00–16:00 and on bank-holiday weekends — go weekday mornings or Sunday afternoons.

Money-saving playbook: ① The £4–5 supermarket meal deal is the single best lunch hack in London — most chains include a coffee. ② Eat your main meal at lunch, not dinner; set lunch menus are 30–50% cheaper. ③ Theatre on the cheap: the TKTS booth on Leicester Square sells same-day West End seats from around £25–40 (and the official TodayTix app does the same). ④ Pubs: a pint is £6–7 in the centre — drink where the workers do, one street off the tourist drag. ⑤ Every museum above is free, which means your whole sightseeing budget can go on food. ⑥ Water: London tap water is excellent — ask for it free in any restaurant, and refill at free water fountains across the centre.

Hashtags to use

#London#VisitLondon#ThisIsLondon#HiddenLondon#LondonLife#NottingHill#BoroughMarket#LondonFoodie#StreetArtLondon#LondonCalling#TimeOutLondon#LoveLondon
Golden hour: sunrise around 05:00–07:00 and sunset 16:00–21:00 depending on the season — search "London sunset time" on the day. Blue hour (20–30 min after sunset) is when Tower Bridge and the South Bank light up.
Beat the crowds: London's photogenic spots are empty before 09:00. Notting Hill at 08:00, Columbia Road at 08:30, Borough Market at 08:00 on a Saturday — same places, no heads in the frame.
Always carry a plan B: it rains. Covered alternatives that still look great: Leadenhall Market, St Pancras, Spitalfields, the museums, and the South Bank under the bridges.
Tag to get featured: @visitlondon and @timeoutlondon repost visitor photos constantly — tag the location and the account and you'll get reposted more often than you'd expect.
Photos: these are real photographs of each place gathered from public image galleries (travel blogs, tourism sites, public wikis) — check licensing before republishing commercially, and swap in your own shots where you can. Trend-watching tip: London trends rotate with the seasons — wisteria on Notting Hill mews in April–May, Columbia Road all summer, autumn foliage in Greenwich and Hampstead in October, Christmas lights on Regent and Oxford Street from mid-November. Check the location tag on Instagram before you go to see which angle is trending this week.
06 — Orientation

The Thames at a Glance

Central London is walkable: the river runs west to east, with the West End (shops, museums, theatres) north of it and the South Bank (Tate Modern, Borough Market) south. Most of the sights on this page sit within a 40-minute walk of each other — or a £1.75 bus ride along the river.

07 — Plan your time

Suggested Itineraries

Three days that lean on everything free, with realistic travel times. Every day below costs under £9 in transport because the daily cap does the work for you.

Day 1 Westminster, the Mall & the South Bank

  1. Westminster Bridge early — the classic Big Ben frame, free and empty before 08:30
  2. Westminster Abbey from Dean's Yard, or attend Evensong later for free
  3. Walk the Mall to Buckingham Palace; Changing the Guard is free (Mon, Wed, Fri 11:00, Sun 10:00)
  4. Trafalgar Square + the free National Gallery (2 hours)
  5. Cross to the South Bank: London Eye (free to look), Southbank Centre food market, Tate Modern (free)
  6. Sunset at Tower Bridge, then pie and mash or a beigel for under £10

Day 2 Museums, Bloomsbury & the City

  1. British Museum at the 10:00 opening (free) — 2–3 hours, Rosetta Stone first
  2. Walk to Covent Garden and Neal's Yard, lunch from the Apple Market stalls or a meal deal
  3. Optional: National Portrait Gallery (free) then St Pancras Renaissance Hotel on the way north
  4. Late afternoon in the City: St Paul's from the outside, Leadenhall Market, Sky Garden or Horizon 22 for sunset (both free, book ahead)
  5. Dinner cheap in Chinatown or Soho (Bao, Kati Roll, Flat Iron)

Day 3 Markets & outlet day

  1. Morning: Borough Market (Wed–Sun) or Columbia Road on a Sunday
  2. Late morning: Brick Lane, Petticoat Lane and Spitalfields — vintage and street art, all walkable
  3. Lunch: street food at Camden or Broadway Market
  4. Afternoon: outlet time — ICON at The O2 or London Designer Outlet on the Jubilee line (or Bicester Village by train for the full designer day)
  5. Evening: Notting Hill at golden hour, or a pub dinner in Camden / a Wetherspoon for £6–9 plates

09 — Know before you go

Practical Tips

1Pay with contactless, never paper. Tap the same card or phone on every journey — in and out on the Tube and trains (buses and trams are tap-in only) — and TfL caps you automatically: £8.90 a day in Zones 1–2, £44.70 Monday–Sunday. Buses are a flat £1.75 with unlimited changes within an hour (the Hopper fare). Paper tickets cost about £7 for the same trip — don't.
2Ride the bus for the view. The bus is cheaper than the Tube, and the front seat upstairs on a route past the West End is the cheapest sightseeing tour in London. Route 11, 24 and 88 are the scenic ones.
3Book the free things first. Sky Garden (Mondays, 3 weeks ahead), Horizon 22 (Mondays 10:00, 14 days) and the free museum tickets go fast. Paid sites needing advance booking: Tower of London (from £37), Buckingham Palace State Rooms (9 July–27 Sept only, £33), Big Ben tower (£55, 11+).
4Stand on the right. Escalator law: stand right, walk left, and let people off the train before you get on. Queue properly everywhere — it's the one thing that will mark you out as a tourist faster than a camera.
5Best seasons: May–June and September are the sweet spots — long days, mild weather, fewer crowds than July–August. December is magical and dark (Christmas lights, winter markets) but hotels cost the most. January–March is the cheapest and quietest for hotels, though it gets dark around 16:15.
6Tipping. Restaurants often add a 12.5% service charge automatically — check the bill, and if it's there you've already tipped. Pubs when ordering at the bar: nothing. Cabs: round up or 5–10%. Free walking tours: £5–10 per person is the norm.
7Bring a Type G plug adapter (three rectangular pins, 230 V) and expect rain at any time of year — pack a compact umbrella and shoes you can walk 20,000 steps in. Layers beat a heavy coat; London weather changes by the hour.
8Safety & scams. London is generally safe and well-policed, but phone-snatching by people on e-bikes is the main risk: don't walk along the kerb with your phone in your hand. Use normal city sense about pickpockets in Oxford Street, Camden and on packed Tube carriages. Ignore anyone who hands you a "free" flower or bracelet, and never buy theatre tickets off a street seller — use TKTS on Leicester Square or the theatre's own site.
9Trains & day trips. Book advance tickets on National Rail apps for Bicester Village, Hampton Court, Windsor or Brighton — an advance off-peak return can cost a fraction of the walk-up fare. A railcard pays for itself in two trips if you qualify, and kids under 5 travel free on the Tube and buses.
10Money & cards. Almost everything is contactless, including market stalls and buses — but keep £10–20 in cash for the smallest vintage traders and donation boxes. The UK has no tourist VAT refund at the airport right now, so plan your shopping around real prices, not an imagined refund.
About this low cost travel & on a budget guide: prices, hours and ratings were collected in September–October 2026 from public sources (museum and attraction websites, TfL fares pages, market operators, review sites) and are approximate — always confirm hours, ticket requirements and prices on the official site before you travel. Museum entry and bus fares change less often than you'd think; special exhibitions and market days change constantly. Car-free tip: you do not need a car in London, and you should not rent one — the congestion charge, parking and ULEZ make it by far the most expensive way to see the city.
